title: Verifier‑Assisted vs. LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether adding a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier (with up to one automated repair) increases the fraction of intent‑driven configuration proposals that pass semantic validation versus accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Each pair used one shared LLM generation (shared_initial) evaluated under two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (validate and permit ≤1 automated repair). Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed=1729, B=10000). The shared_initial estimand conditions on a single LLM candidate per intent and therefore isolates verifier+repair effects for that candidate (it does not capture benefits from independent alternative candidate draws per condition). Under the chosen synthetic suite and model, single‑shot generation was near ceiling, leaving minimal room for guarded rescue; raw execution and analysis artifacts are archived with the run.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. Practical deployment of LLM‑generated changes requires pre‑deployment semantic checks because syntactic correctness alone does not guarantee safety (reachability, policy preservation, required sequencing). Prior work suggests generate→validate→repair scaffolds can reduce errors, but reported benefits vary with model power, task hardness, and validator semantics. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment that isolates the marginal effect of a deterministic verifier (plus a bounded repair budget) on an identical LLM candidate per intent. Research question: Does integrating a deterministic verifier into an LLM‑driven change‑generation pipeline increase the probability that an LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation (unflagged) compared with accepting a single‑shot LLM output when both conditions evaluate the same candidate? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation (N=300 pairs) conditioning on a single shared_initial candidate to measure verifier/repair rescue utility; (2) fully archived execution and analysis demonstrating a near‑ceiling baseline on the supplied synthetic suite with gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (3) careful discussion of estimand selection, statistical interpretation in near‑ceiling settings, threats to validity, and operational recommendations for follow‑up studies.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and systems work document active effort applying LLMs to NetOps tasks (intent translation, template synthesis, repair) and developing tool‑augmented agentic frameworks to enable verifier and tool calls. Representative findings from the verified literature: (a) LLMs can synthesize configuration artifacts and intent translations but performance varies by task and dataset; (b) planner‑centric and tool‑augmented pipelines enable external validators to be invoked to check semantics and to guide repairs; (c) generate→validate→repair patterns often reduce errors relative to unconstrained generation, though gains depend on validator coverage and model quality; (d) detection and mitigation approaches (entropy‑based detectors, deterministic safety nets, retrieval augmentation, self‑reflection) combat hallucination but transferability to complex NetOps remains limited. Our study complements these lines by evaluating a bounded verifier+repair intervention under a preregistered paired estimand that isolates rescue of a single shared candidate. (Representative verified sources used for positioning are cited at the end of the paper.)
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand: The study preregistration (id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) specified a confirmatory paired design with 300 analyzable pairs (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high), a shared_initial generation per pair, and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in proportion of unflagged verifier passes between guarded and baseline conditions). Key frozen design choices: declared model = gpt-5-mini; validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 using the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule; baseline condition = accept the shared_initial LLM output as final; guarded condition = run deterministic validator and, if it fails, permit at most one automated repair attempt followed by revalidation; repair budget per pair ≤1. The shared_initial protocol means both conditions evaluate the same single candidate per pair, isolating the verifier/repair effect conditional on that candidate (see Discussion for implications). Planned episodes and stopping rules: planned_episode_count = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions). The run stops when 300 analyzable pairs are obtained per preregistered exclusion rules; pairs are excluded only if both pipeline calls fail due to provider/infrastructure outage (no such dual failures occurred). Analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 implementing an exact two‑sided McNemar‑equivalent conditional test and a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10000, bootstrap_seed=1729). Pilot status: the preregistration included a pilot (n=60) for discordance estimation and power calibration; that pilot was not executed and no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed—the main N=300 was used as pre‑specified. Execution provenance: the run executed under the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared_initial calls, 1 repair call); planned_episode_count = 600 and completed_episode_count = 600. Inclusion/exclusion, missingness and contamination controls were implemented as preregistered and produced no excluded pairs or contamination flags.
sections.results: Execution accounting: the run started at 2026-08-30T09:47:41.113164+00:00 and completed at 2026-08-30T10:17:21.408465+00:00 (execution manifest). Completed episodes = 600 (300 pairs), model_calls_used = 301, stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 1. Condition margins (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 299/300 (0.9966667), guarded successes = 300/300 (1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 299 (both pass), n10 = 1 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 0 (both fail). Confirmatory inference (paired_binary_analysis_v1): absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Per‑stratum outcomes: baseline — low 100/100, medium 100/100, high 99/100; guarded — 100/100 in each stratum. Repair and rescue: a single guarded episode invoked the allowed automated repair and converted a baseline‑flagged candidate into a guarded pass (the lone discordant observation, n10 = 1). The archived validator traces indicate the automated repair inserted the required sequencing step (an explicit 'admin down' before changing VLAN/MTU) to satisfy the validator's must_be_down_for_fields workflow rule; after insertion the deterministic validator reported valid == true. Representative artifacts illustrating the format of tasks, required_sequence policies, and the validator trace for that rescued episode are archived in the run bundle (task manifest entries and validator traces). Missingness and contamination: no episodes were excluded and contamination_summary.csv is empty.
sections.discussion: Statistical and practical interpretation: The observed absolute paired improvement (0.00333) is numerically small because single‑shot LLM generation already satisfied the deterministic validator in 299 of 300 paired intents. The exact two‑sided McNemar test produced p = 1.0 given m = n10 + n01 = 1 discordant observation; this high p value reflects paucity of discordant evidence rather than evidence of equality. The 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] bounds the plausible paired improvement under the shared_initial estimand to ≤1 percentage point in this setting. Estimand implications: the shared_initial design isolates deterministic rescue/repair effects conditional on the same LLM candidate; it intentionally excludes verifier benefits that would accrue from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (for example, if a verifier guided a model to produce different initial candidates). Operational implications: when base models are near‑ceiling relative to a given validator suite, the marginal correctness gain from a bounded verifier+repair intervention (under shared_initial) may be small, but deterministic validation still provides auditability and a deterministic mechanism for targeted repair of specific workflow violations. Recommendations for follow‑ups: evaluate (a) independent draws per condition (to measure end‑to‑end pipeline gains), (b) weaker LLMs or intentionally harder/realistic intents to increase discordance, and (c) richer repair budgets and ensemble repair strategies to quantify repair cost/benefit tradeoffs. Failure‑mode diagnostics: on the supplied synthetic suite, the dominant flagged failure class was sequencing/ordering violations (must_be_down_for_fields) that the validator deterministically detected; automated repair success depended on a syntactic insertion that restored required sequencing. This pattern suggests validator design that exposes explicit workflow constraints can make automated repairs effective for localized ordering errors but may be less effective for semantic omissions or hallucinated nonexistent resources.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate (shared_initial) on a 300‑pair synthetic NetOps benchmark using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Baseline single‑shot generation achieved 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding a negligible paired improvement (0.00333; paired McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% CI [0.00,0.01]). These results demonstrate that measured verifier marginality depends strongly on base model capability, task difficulty, validator semantics, and estimand conditioning. We release the preregistration id, execution and analysis artifacts, representative task manifests, and validator traces in the archived run bundle to support community replication and to encourage follow‑up studies that vary model strength, estimand choice, and repair budgets.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/verifier‑diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to the preregistered target (10 percentage points).
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot (n=60) intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration recalculation of required sample size was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition.
Repair budget: guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
